description: We are engineering students from Berkeley interested in building tools that help people!
summary:
Rice farmers can save water and cut methane by letting fields dry between irrigations. But someone has to check whether that happened. Mudskipper uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar to help inspectors decide where to look.

Mudskipper addresses “Dancing with the SARs” by using NISAR radar data to track and visualize flooding and drainage in Punjab’s rice fields over time.  Because satellites only observe fields on certain dates, and so some drainage events may go undetected. Mudskipper accounts for these uncertainties so users can see how reliable the evidence is for each field. Our current analysis covers 5,000 estimated field segments across two regions in Punjab by using NISAR radar observations from nine different dates. 

Of these, 840 show signs of alternate wetting and drying (AWD), a practice that lets fields drain between irrigations, while 321 show patterns inconsistent with AWD. The remaining 3,839 do not have enough evidence to reach a conclusion. The goal of Mudskipper is to help agricultural agencies and carbon-credit auditors decide where to inspect first.
details:
What the project does:


A farmer can let a rice field dry between irrigations to save water and reduce methane. For the people funding those changes, checking what happened across thousands of fields is a difficult job. Field visits take time, and monsoon clouds block the view from optical satellites.

We built a Mudskipper to help inspectors choose where to look. It uses radar observations from NASA-ISRO's NISAR satellite to build a record of likely flooding and drainage in two study areas in Punjab, India. Radar works through clouds. Its longer L-band wavelength can also provide information about water beneath rice plants.

The app lets users move from a regional map to an individual field segment and replay the available satellite dates. It reports whether the season looks consistent with alternate wetting and drying (AWD). When the observations cannot settle the question, it reports "not enough evidence." An inspection tool then ranks submitted claims for follow-up.

Our intended users are subsidy officials, carbon-credit verifiers, and field inspection teams. Developers can use the same results through a public API, a way for other software to request the data.


How it works:

Mudskipper starts with NISAR radar data placed on a map grid, supplied through NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility. The Python pipeline measures the radar signal over each field segment. It uses statistical models and changes in the signal over time to estimate whether the segment appears flooded/drained/uncertain. Some July observations also combine evidence from Europe's Sentinel-1 radar satellite.

The interpretation changes as the crop grows. Early in the season, smooth standing water often reflects radar away from the satellite and looks dark. Later, water and plant stems can produce a stronger return. That is why one brightness rule cannot explain the whole season.

A separate simulation tests what the available satellite dates could detect. It creates drainage scenarios and asks how often those dates would catch them, using published research and stated assumptions. The verdict rules use these estimates to decide when the evidence supports a conclusion.  

The published run contains 5,000 provisional field segments, nine NISAR satellites  passed from July 2 to October 18, 2026, and 45,000 observations. The model gives 840 segments a result consistent with AWD and 321 an inconsistent result. It leaves 3,839, about 77%, undecided.

Mudskipper prioritizes 80% of field inspections based on satellite evidence and field size. The remaining 20% are chosen randomly within each district, so fields that appear less suspicious still have a chance of being inspected.


Benefits and intended impact:

Water-saving rice programs need a reliable way to check how farmers manage irrigation. Mudskipper helps inspectors understand what happened in each field before visiting it. They can review satellite observations and identify fields where the evidence needs closer attention.

This could help agricultural agencies make better use of limited inspection resources. It also makes the process fairer for farmers. Satellites cannot observe fields continuously, so a drainage event might happen between observation dates. Mudskipper accounts for this uncertainty rather than treating missing data as evidence that a farmer failed to follow irrigation practices.

Tools and technology:

Mudskipper's radar processing pipeline uses Python, NumPy, scikit-learn, Rasterio, and geospatial libraries to analyze NISAR satellite data. It converts radar images into measurements for individual field segments. Our current analysis uses estimated field segments with separate workflow using Fields of the World tools also used to improve field boundaries.

The backend uses a shared TypeScript engine to evaluate irrigation patterns and simulate what satellites could have observed. The same engine also determines which fields should be inspected first. Both the website and API use these rules to produce consistent results. JSON Schema validates data exchanged between the Python and TypeScript systems.

The website is built with Vite, TypeScript, React, Astryx, and StyleX.

GitHub Actions runs automated Python and TypeScript tests. We use Playwright and axe to test the website across screen sizes and check keyboard accessibility.


Creativity and originality:

Mudskipper lets users explore an entire rice-growing season through satellite radar data. They can zoom from a regional map into individual fields and replay how estimated flooding and drainage patterns changed over time.

Our interactive lab shows what satellites might miss. Users can adjust drainage cycles to see how a field could dry out and flood again between satellite observations. Animated radar scenes also explain how water and rice plants affect the signals detected from space.

Inspectors can then use these findings to decide which fields need a closer look. This is especially useful when satellite observations alone cannot tell the full story.


Design considerations

Mudskipper could eventually help make decisions about farmers' payments, so we need to be careful about what the satellite data can actually prove. NISAR typically observes the same area every 12 days, and there was a data gap between July 27 and August 10, 2026.  

Our study focuses on two areas of roughly 15 × 15 kilometres in Fazilka and Sri Muktsar Sahib. The field outlines are estimated from satellite images rather than surveyed boundaries, so our findings should not be taken as representative of either district as a whole.

We also compare our findings with NASA's OPERA DSWx-S1 surface-water maps, which use Sentinel-1 radar at 30-metre resolution. However, the two satellites detect water differently, especially beneath rice plants. Some of our July estimates also rely on Sentinel-1 data, meaning those comparisons are not entirely independent. Any disagreements still need to be investigated on the ground.

We designed the website to work on smaller screens and support keyboard navigation. Users can control animations, and important information is not communicated through colour alone. Automated accessibility tests check relevant WCAG 2.2 A and AA requirements.
